## Chapter 1 — The Counterpane

Upon waking next morning about daylight, I found Queequeg's arm thrown over me in the most loving and affectionate manner. You had almost thought I had been his wife. The counterpane was of patchwork, full of odd little parti-coloured squares and triangles; and this arm of his tattooed all over with an interminable Cretan labyrinth of a figure—looked for all the world like a strip of that same patchwork quilt. Partly lying on it as I was, I could hardly tell it from the quilt.

My sensations were strange. When I was a child, I well remember a somewhat similar circumstance. For some mischief, my stepmother packed me off to bed at two o'clock on the 21st June, the longest day of the year. I lay there dismally calculating that sixteen entire hours must elapse before I could hope for a resurrection. At last I fell into a troubled doze; and waking—the sun-lit room now wrapped in outer darkness—I felt a shock running through all my frame; a supernatural hand seemed placed in mine. My arm hung over the counterpane, and the nameless, unimaginable, silent form to which the hand belonged seemed closely seated by my bed-side. For what seemed ages piled on ages, I lay there frozen with the most awful fears, not daring to drag away my hand. To this very hour, I often puzzle myself with it.

Now, take away the awful fear, and my sensations at feeling Queequeg's pagan arm thrown round me were very similar in their strangeness. I strove to rouse him—"Queequeg!"—but his only answer was a snore. Throwing aside the counterpane, there lay the tomahawk sleeping by the savage's side, as if it were a hatchet-faced baby. At length, by dint of much wriggling, I extracted a grunt; he drew back his arm, shook himself all over like a Newfoundland dog, and sat up stiff as a pike-staff.

He commenced dressing at top by donning his beaver hat; then—still minus his trowsers—he crushed himself under the bed to put on his boots. He was just enough civilized to show off his outlandishness in the strangest possible manners—a creature in the transition stage, neither caterpillar nor butterfly. For his toilet, he took the harpoon from the bed-corner, whetted it on his boot, and strode up to the mirror, beginning a vigorous harpooning of his cheeks. The rest was soon achieved; he marched out wrapped in his pilot monkey jacket, sporting his harpoon like a marshal's baton.

## Chapter 2 — Breakfast

I quickly followed suit, and descending into the bar-room accosted the grinning landlord very pleasantly. A good laugh is a mighty good thing, and rather too scarce a good thing.

The bar-room was full of boarders—chief mates, harpooneers, ship keepers; a brown and brawny company, with bosky beards, all wearing monkey jackets for morning gowns. You could pretty plainly tell how long each one had been ashore by the hue of his cheek. But who could show a cheek like Queequeg's?—barred with various tints, like the Andes' western slope, contrasting climates zone by zone.

"Grub, ho!" cried the landlord, and in we went to breakfast. To my no small surprise, nearly every man maintained a profound silence. Here were sea-dogs who had boarded great whales on the high seas and duelled them dead without winking; yet here they sat looking as sheepishly at each other as though they had never been out of sight of some sheepfold among the Green Mountains.

But Queequeg—Queequeg sat there at the head of the table, cool as an icicle; reaching over with his harpoon to grapple the beefsteaks towards him. That was certainly very coolly done; and every one knows that to do anything coolly is to do it genteelly.

## Chapter 3 — The Street

The streets of New Bedford beat all Water Street and Wapping. In those last-mentioned haunts you see only sailors; but in New Bedford, actual cannibals stand chatting at street corners; savages outright; many of whom yet carry on their bones unholy flesh. It makes a stranger stare.

Besides the Feegeeans, Tongatobooarrs, and Erromanggoans, you will see other sights still more comical. There weekly arrive scores of green Vermonters and New Hampshire men, all athirst for gain and glory in the fishery. Many are as green as the Green Mountains whence they came. No town-bred dandy will compare with a downright bumpkin dandy—a fellow that will mow his two acres in buckskin gloves for fear of tanning his hands.

Yet New Bedford has more than cannibals and bumpkins. Nowhere in all America will you find more patrician-like houses, parks and gardens more opulent. Whence came they? how planted upon this once scraggy scoria of a country? Go and gaze upon the iron emblematical harpoons round yonder lofty mansion, and your question will be answered. All these brave houses were harpooned and dragged up hither from the bottom of the sea.

And the women of New Bedford, they bloom like their own red roses. But roses only bloom in summer; whereas the fine carnation of their cheeks is perennial as sunlight in the seventh heavens.

## Chapter 4 — The Chapel

In New Bedford stands a Whaleman's Chapel. Wrapping myself in my shaggy bearskin, I fought against the stubborn storm. Entering, I found a small scattered congregation of sailors, and sailors' wives and widows. A muffled silence reigned, broken only by the shrieks of the storm. Each silent worshipper sat apart, as if each grief were insular and incommunicable. On the walls beside the pulpit, marble tablets with black borders memorialized the lost—swallowed overboard near the Isle of Desolation, towed out of sight by a whale in the Pacific, killed in the bows of his boat on the coast of Japan. Queequeg alone seemed struck by wondering curiosity, for he alone could not read.

What bitter blanks in those black-bordered marbles which cover no ashes! What despair in those immovable inscriptions! But Faith, like a jackal, feeds among the tombs, and even from these dead doubts she gathers her most vital hope.

Yes, Ishmael, the same fate may be thine. But somehow I grew merry again. Methinks we have hugely mistaken this matter of Life and Death. Methinks that what they call my shadow here on earth is my true substance; my body is but the lees of my better being. Three cheers for Nantucket; come a stove boat and stove body when they will, for stave my soul, Jove himself cannot.

## Chapter 5 — The Pulpit

I had not been seated long ere a man of venerable robustness entered—the famous Father Mapple, a great favourite among the whalemen, who had been a sailor and harpooneer in his youth. He was in the hardy winter of a healthy old age; a second flowering youth peeping forth from among the fissures of his wrinkles. His tarpaulin hat ran down with melting sleet, his great pilot jacket heavy with absorbed water.

Arrayed in a decent suit, he approached the pulpit—a very lofty one, mounted by a perpendicular side ladder like those used in boarding a ship at sea. Father Mapple mounted hand over hand; having gained the height, he deliberately dragged up the ladder step by step, till he was impregnable in his little Quebec. By that act of physical isolation he signified his spiritual withdrawal from all outward worldly ties.

Behind the pulpit hung a painting of a gallant ship beating against a terrible storm; high above, a little isle of sunlight shed an angel's face upon the tossed deck. The pulpit itself was in the likeness of a ship's bluff bows, the Bible resting on scroll work fashioned after a ship's fiddle-headed beak. The pulpit is ever this earth's foremost part; all the rest comes in its rear; the pulpit leads the world. The world's a ship on its passage out, and not a voyage complete; and the pulpit is its prow.

## Chapter 6 — The Sermon

Father Mapple rose, and in a mild voice of unassuming authority ordered the scattered people to condense. "Starboard gangway, there! side away to larboard—larboard gangway to starboard! Midships! midships!"

He knelt in the pulpit's bows, folded his hands, and offered a prayer so deeply devout that he seemed kneeling at the bottom of the sea. Then, in prolonged solemn tones like the tolling of a bell in a foundering ship, he commenced the hymn, bursting out in its final stanzas with pealing exultation:

"The ribs and terrors in the whale,
Arched over me a dismal gloom,
While all God's sun-lit waves rolled by,
And lift me deepening down to doom.

"My song for ever shall record
That terrible, that joyful hour;
I give the glory to my God,
His all the mercy and the power."

Then he said: "Beloved shipmates, clinch the last verse of the first chapter of Jonah—'And God had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah.' Shipmates, this book is one of the smallest strands in the mighty cable of the Scriptures. Yet what depths of the soul does Jonah's deep sealine sound! It is a two-stranded lesson: a lesson to us all as sinful men, and a lesson to me as a pilot of the living God. If we obey God, we must disobey ourselves; and it is in this disobeying ourselves, wherein the hardness of obeying God consists.

"Jonah flouts at God by seeking to flee from Him. He skulks about the wharves of Joppa, and seeks a ship bound for Tarshish. Jonah's Captain was one whose discernment detects crime in any, but whose cupidity exposes it only in the penniless. In this world, sin that pays its way can travel freely, and without a passport; whereas Virtue, if a pauper, is stopped at all frontiers. The Captain charges him thrice the usual sum, and Jonah assents.

"In his state-room, a swinging lamp maintains a permanent obliquity with the heeling ship; though, in truth, infallibly straight itself, it but made obvious the false, lying levels among which it hung. 'Oh!' he groans, 'so my conscience hangs in me! straight upwards, so it burns; but the chambers of my soul are all in crookedness!'

"A dreadful storm comes on; Jonah, below, sleeps his hideous sleep. The master shrieks in his dead ear, 'What meanest thou, O, sleeper! arise!' The sailors cast lots; the lot is Jonah's. Forced by the hard hand of God upon him, he cries—'I am a Hebrew; I fear the Lord the God of Heaven who hath made the sea and the dry land!' He bids them cast him forth into the sea. They lay hold of him and dropped him; instantly an oily calmness floats out, and the whale shoots-to all his ivory teeth upon his prison. Then Jonah prayed unto the Lord out of the fish's belly. Sinful as he is, Jonah does not weep for deliverance; he leaves all his deliverance to God. And here, shipmates, is true and faithful repentance; not clamorous for pardon, but grateful for punishment."

While he spoke, the howling storm seemed to add new power to the preacher; his tossed arms seemed the warring elements at work. Then, lowering his head in deepest humility, he spake the other lesson—how Jonah, bidden to preach to Nineveh, had fled his mission; how God came upon him in the whale; how, out of the belly of hell, when Jonah cried, God spake unto the fish, and Jonah did the Almighty's bidding—to preach the Truth to the face of Falsehood!

"This is that other lesson; and woe to that pilot of the living God who slights it. Woe to him whom this world charms from Gospel duty! Woe to him who seeks to pour oil upon the waters when God has brewed them into a gale! Woe to him whose good name is more to him than goodness! Woe to him who would not be true, even though to be false were salvation!"

Then, a deep joy in his eyes, he cried: "But oh! shipmates! on the starboard hand of every woe, there is a sure delight. Delight is to him who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth, ever stands forth his own inexorable self. Delight is to him whose strong arms yet support him, when the ship of this base treacherous world has gone down beneath him. Delight is to him who acknowledges no law or lord but the Lord his God, and is only a patriot to heaven. And eternal delight and deliciousness will be his, who coming to lay him down, can say with his final breath—O Father!—mortal or immortal, here I die. I have striven to be Thine, more than to be this world's, or mine own."

He said no more, but slowly waving a benediction, covered his face with his hands, and so remained kneeling, till all the people had departed, and he was left alone in the place.

## Chapter 7 — A Bosom Friend

Returning to the Spouter-Inn, I found Queequeg quite alone, sitting before the fire, holding his little negro idol close up to his face and gently whittling away at its nose, humming in his heathenish way. Being interrupted, he put up the image and took up a large book, counting the pages with deliberate regularity; at every fiftieth page stopping, giving utterance to a long-drawn gurgling whistle of astonishment.

Savage though he was, and hideously marred about the face, his countenance had a something in it which was by no means disagreeable. You cannot hide the soul. Through all his unearthly tattooings, I saw the traces of a simple honest heart; and in his large, deep eyes, fiery black and bold, tokens of a spirit that would dare a thousand devils. Queequeg was George Washington cannibalistically developed.

Here was a man some twenty thousand miles from home, by way of Cape Horn, thrown among people as strange to him as though he were in the planet Jupiter; yet he seemed entirely at his ease, content with his own companionship, always equal to himself. I began to feel myself mysteriously drawn towards him. I'll try a pagan friend, thought I, since Christian kindness has proved but hollow courtesy.

I drew my bench near him, and made some friendly signs. We turned over the book together, and soon were exchanging puffs from his tomahawk-pipe. This pleasant, genial smoke thawed any ice of indifference in the Pagan's breast, and left us cronies. When our smoke was over, he pressed his forehead against mine, clasped me round the waist, and said that henceforth we were married; meaning, in his country's phrase, that we were bosom friends; he would gladly die for me, if need should be.

He made me a present of his embalmed head; then, drawing thirty dollars in silver from his tobacco wallet, divided them into two portions and pushed one towards me. I let them stay. Then he began his evening prayers. I was a good Christian, born and bred in the bosom of the infallible Presbyterian Church. How could I unite with this wild idolator in worshipping his piece of wood? But what is worship?—to do the will of God—_that_ is worship. And what is the will of God?—to do to my fellow man what I would have my fellow man to do to me—_that_ is the will of God. Now, Queequeg is my fellow man; ergo, I must turn idolator. So I kindled the shavings; helped prop up the little idol; salamed before him; kissed his nose; and that done, we undressed and went to bed, at peace with our own consciences and all the world.

There is no place like a bed for confidential disclosures between friends. Thus, in our hearts' honeymoon, lay I and Queequeg—a cosy, loving pair.

## Chapter 8 — Nightgown

We had lain chatting and napping, Queequeg now and then affectionately throwing his brown tattooed legs over mine, so sociable and free and easy were we; till at last what little nappishness remained in us altogether departed. We found ourselves sitting up, leaning against the head-board with our knees drawn up, our noses bending over them as if our kneepans were warming-pans. Very nice and snug it was, the more so since it was so chilly out of doors.

Truly to enjoy bodily warmth, some small part of you must be cold, for there is no quality in this world that is not what it is merely by contrast. Nothing exists in itself. If you flatter yourself you are all over comfortable, you cannot be said to be comfortable any more. But if, like Queequeg and me in the bed, the tip of your nose be slightly chilled, why then, indeed, you feel most delightfully and unmistakably warm.

Upon opening my eyes, coming out of my own pleasant and self-created darkness into the coarse outer gloom of the unilluminated twelve-o'clock-at-night, I experienced a disagreeable revulsion. No man can ever feel his own identity aright except his eyes be closed; as if darkness were indeed the proper element of our essences, though light be more congenial to our clayey part.

So we struck a light; and Queequeg, eager for a few quiet puffs from his Tomahawk, began to speak of his native island.

## Chapter 9 — Biographical

Queequeg was a native of Rokovoko, an island far away to the West and South. It is not down in any map; true places never are.

His father was a High Chief, a King. A Sag Harbor ship visited his father's bay, and Queequeg sought a passage to Christian lands. Denied, he paddled his canoe to a distant strait the ship must pass; as she glided by, darted out, capsized beneath him, climbed the chains, and threw himself upon the deck, grappling a ring-bolt and swearing not to let go though hacked in pieces. The captain at last relented.

At bottom, he desired to learn among the Christians the arts whereby to make his people happier and better than they were. But the practices of whalemen soon convinced him that even Christians could be both miserable and wicked. Thought he, it's a wicked world in all meridians; I'll die a pagan.

They had made a harpooneer of him, and that barbed iron was in lieu of a sceptre now. When I told him whaling was my own design—to sail out of Nantucket—he at once resolved to accompany me, ship aboard the same vessel, the same boat, the same mess, to share my every hap. To all this I joyously assented; for besides the affection I now felt for Queequeg, he was an experienced harpooneer, and could not fail to be of great usefulness to one so wholly ignorant of the mysteries of whaling.

His story ended with his pipe's last dying puff; Queequeg embraced me, pressed his forehead against mine, and blowing out the light, we rolled over and very soon were sleeping.
